narrative.h2: Hip hop video carries a city on its shoulders

sections.heading: What hip hop looks like
sections.body: Hip hop MVs braid two layers: the performance — usually the rapper to camera, lip-synced tight, often in a powerful low angle — and the world that produced the song. That world is specific. Compton, Houston, Toronto, Brooklyn each have a visual signature, and the best videos refuse to be from nowhere. Wardrobe is current to the month, not the year. Cars matter. Crews matter. Cuts land on the rhyme, never the beat alone.

sections.heading: Reference points that actually work
sections.body: Kendrick Lamar's 'HUMBLE.' and 'Alright' (both directed by Dave Meyers and the little homies) are the modern textbook for performance plus social weight. Travis Scott's 'SICKO MODE' and 'HIGHEST IN THE ROOM' (Dave Meyers again) show surreal scale without losing rap as the spine. Hiro Murai's work with Donald Glover ('This Is America', 'Sober') and FKA Twigs raised the bar for narrative MVs. J. Cole's 'MIDDLE CHILD' keeps it conversational; Drake's 'Hotline Bling' directed by Director X went minimalist and changed everything. Cole Bennett's Lyrical Lemonade visuals for Juice WRLD and Eminem extend the lineage, with Hype Williams' fisheye era and Spike Jonze's Beastie Boys work as the ground rules.

sections.heading: Prompting tip for Tunee
sections.body: Give Tunee a specific neighborhood, not a generic city. 'Late-evening porch in South Memphis, two friends, blue twilight' beats 'urban street scene' every time. Lock down one signature wardrobe element — chain, hoodie, hat — and let it appear in every cut so the artist reads as continuous. Use the verse-chorus structure: tight performance frames during bars, B-roll lifestyle during the hook. Cut on the consonants, not the kick.
